tip: Fixing the colours of a video so they look natural and match from shot to shot.
meaning: Color correction repairs problems: a picture that is too dark, too blue or too yellow. The goal is for white to look white and skin to look like skin.
example: A video filmed indoors looks orange, so you make it a little cooler.
vukem: `clip.set_color` sets brightness, contrast and saturation. See [Effects and color](/docs/guide/effects-and-color).

tip: Giving a video a chosen look and mood with colour, on top of the correction.
meaning: After the colours are right, grading makes them tell a feeling: warm and golden for a happy memory, cold and blue for a sad one.
example: A movie about the desert is graded orange and yellow.

tip: How light or dark the whole picture is.
meaning: Raising brightness makes every part of the picture lighter, so the dark parts also turn grey. Use it gently.
example: A video filmed in shade made brighter so the face is visible.

tip: The difference between the darkest and the lightest parts of the picture.
meaning: A high contrast picture has deep blacks and bright whites. A low contrast one looks flat and grey, like on a foggy day.
example: A foggy video looks better with a bit more contrast.

tip: How strong or pale the colours are.
meaning: At full saturation colours are rich and strong. At zero there is no colour at all and the picture is black and white.
example: Turn saturation down and a rainbow fades to grey.

tip: The pure colour itself: red, orange, yellow, green, blue or purple.
meaning: Hue is the name of the colour, apart from how strong or light it is. Moving the hue turns reds into greens, for example.
example: Changing a red car into a blue car by moving its hue.

tip: Setting what counts as white, so colours don't look too blue or too orange.
meaning: Light has a colour: candles are orange, shade is blue. White balance tells the camera what white looks like in that light so the other colours come out right.
example: In a room lit by warm bulbs, a white wall looks orange until the white balance is set.

tip: How warm (orange) or cool (blue) a light or a picture looks, in kelvins.
meaning: Low numbers like 2700 K are warm and orange, like a candle. High numbers like 6500 K are cool and blueish, like daylight on a cloudy day.
example: A sunset is warm; a clear sky is cool.

tip: A little green or pink pushed over the whole picture.
meaning: Tint is the other slider next to temperature. It moves the picture between green and magenta, to remove a colour cast.
example: A video under a fluorescent light looks a bit green, so you add some pink.

tip: The bright, medium and dark parts of a picture.
meaning: Editors treat the three parts separately. Highlights are the brightest areas, shadows the darkest and midtones everything in between.
example: Lower the highlights so the sky does not turn pure white.

tip: A setting that makes the middle tones lighter or darker without touching black and white.
meaning: Gamma changes how bright the middle of the picture is, while the darkest and the lightest points stay the same.
example: A picture that looks too dark in the middle is helped by raising the gamma.

tip: A graph that shows how many dark, medium and bright pixels there are.
meaning: A histogram is a little mountain chart. Mountains on the left mean a dark picture, on the right a bright one. It tells you if the picture is too dark or too bright without trusting your eyes.
example: A tall mountain stuck at the right edge means parts are pure white.

tip: A scope that shows how bright every part of the picture is.
meaning: A waveform monitor plots brightness across the picture. Editors use it to keep white from burning and black from turning into mud.
example: Checking that the sky does not go above the top line.

tip: A scope that shows which colours there are and how strong they are.
meaning: A vectorscope is a round chart. The further a dot is from the middle, the stronger its colour. It helps to keep skin tones looking natural.
example: A line on the chart shows where human skin should fall.

tip: A file that changes colours in one go, like a ready-made photo filter.
meaning: A LUT (look-up table) is a recipe: for every input colour, it says which colour to show. Editors use LUTs to apply a look or to convert a flat camera picture to a normal one.
example: Dropping a "warm film" LUT on a clip to give it a movie look.
vukem: Import a .cube file as a lut asset and apply it to a clip with clip.set_color (lut_asset and lut_intensity).

tip: The overall colour style of a video.
meaning: A look is how colours, contrast and grain are combined to give a particular style, such as "old film" or "clean and bright".
example: A "vintage" look makes your video seem like an old home movie.

tip: A rule that says which numbers mean which colours.
meaning: A colour space is a map between numbers and colours. If a video is saved with one map and played with another, the colours look wrong.
example: A photo that looks dull on one screen and vivid on another may be using a different colour space.

tip: The range of colours a screen or a format is able to show.
meaning: A wide gamut can show very strong greens and reds. A small gamut cannot. Colours outside the gamut are squeezed in.
example: A new phone can show richer greens than an old office screen.

tip: The standard colour space of the web and most screens.
meaning: sRGB is the colour map most computers and websites assume. If nobody says otherwise, an image is treated as sRGB.
example: Photos on websites are usually sRGB.

tip: The standard colour and brightness rules for normal HD video.
meaning: Rec. 709 is the long-time standard for HD television and most web video. Its colours are about the same as sRGB.
example: A YouTube HD video is normally Rec. 709.

tip: A wider colour standard used for 4K and HDR video.
meaning: Rec. 2020 can show many more colours than Rec. 709. It is used for ultra-high-definition video.
example: A 4K HDR film from a streaming service.

tip: How many steps of each colour a file can store, like 8-bit or 10-bit.
meaning: More bits give smoother gradients. With too few, a sky can show ugly steps called banding.
example: A blue sky going from light to dark looks like stripes in 8 bits but smooth in 10 bits.

tip: Visible stripes in a smooth colour, like a sky.
meaning: When a gradient has too few colour steps, your eye sees bands instead of a smooth fade. It is more visible after heavy compression.
example: A sunset sky shows rings of orange instead of a smooth glow.

tip: The range from the darkest to the brightest thing a camera or a screen can show.
meaning: High dynamic range means you can see both the dark corner of a room and the bright window at once, instead of one being black or white.
example: A camera with a big dynamic range shows clouds and a face at the same time.

tip: High dynamic range: brighter brights and deeper darks than normal video.
meaning: HDR video can show much brighter highlights and richer colours than usual (SDR) video, on a screen that supports it.
example: Sun glints on water that look really bright on an HDR phone.

tip: Standard dynamic range: the ordinary range of normal video.
meaning: SDR is the normal look of most video for the last decades. It has less bright highlights than HDR.
example: A regular YouTube video is SDR.

tip: Flat, grey-looking video from a camera, made to keep more detail for colour work.
meaning: Log recording keeps both dark and bright details but looks washed out. You are supposed to add contrast and colour later.
example: A professional camera video looks dull on purpose until it is graded.

tip: Storing colour with fewer details than brightness to make files smaller.
meaning: Eyes see brightness sharper than colour, so videos often store full detail for brightness and a quarter of the detail for colour. This is written 4:2:0.
example: A tiny red text on a green background looks fuzzier in video than in a photo.

tip: Luma is brightness; chroma is colour.
meaning: Video often keeps the brightness (luma) and the colour (chroma) in separate parts. A black-and-white picture is only luma.
example: A black and white TV shows only luma.

tip: Making every colour by mixing red, green and blue light.
meaning: Screens make colours from tiny red, green and blue lights. Mix them all and you get white, turn them all off and you get black.
example: Red and green lights together make yellow.

tip: A small note inside a file that says which colour rules it uses.
meaning: A profile tells the program how to read the colours of an image or video, so they look the same on different devices.
example: A photo that looks the same on your phone and your computer.

tip: A picture with only greys, no colour.
meaning: Grayscale (black and white) keeps brightness and removes all colour. It is often used for an old-time look.
example: An old photograph.

tip: A warm brown tint that makes a picture look old.
meaning: Sepia colours the picture in brown tones like old photographs.
example: A picture of your grandparents made to look like it is a hundred years old.

tip: Darkening the corners of a picture to draw the eye to the middle.
meaning: A vignette is a soft dark ring around the edges. It makes the subject in the middle stand out.
example: A portrait where the corners fade to black.
